analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from forcing retirement plan participants into arbitration or waiving their right to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by any committee or given a vote, and it ended the 118th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal retirement-benefit law (ERISA) so that employers and plan administrators could no longer force workers and retirees to settle disputes over their benefits in private arbitration, sign away their right to join class-action lawsuits, or give plan administrators unchecked discretion to decide benefits. Those clauses are commonly written into 401(k) and pension plan documents today. Instead, participants could take their claims to a regular court.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees with employer-sponsored retirement or benefit plans. Under current law, plan documents often include fine-print clauses requiring any dispute over benefits to be decided by a private arbitrator rather than a court, waiving the right to join a class action, and letting the plan administrator decide benefits with only deferential court review. The bill would make all of those clauses unenforceable and prohibit plans from including them, so participants could sue in court, as a group where appropriate, and get a fresh judicial review of disputed benefit decisions [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees in benefit plans

how_it_helps.text: Makes pre-dispute mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable for ERISA plan claims, so a participant who loses benefits can go to court instead of a private arbitrator [S2].
Nullifies class-action and representation waivers, preserving the right to join or bring group claims against plan sponsors and administrators [S2].

Allows post-dispute arbitration only under strict conditions: no coercion, a plain-language written notice, a 45-day waiting period, and affirmative written consent, with no retaliation for refusing [S2].
Bans 'discretionary clauses' that let plan administrators control how courts review benefit decisions, restoring full de novo court review of disputed determinations [S2].

Ensures disputes over whether an arbitration clause is valid are decided by a judge, not the arbitrator, and applies the changes to existing plan documents without a waiting period for the protections themselves [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, plan sponsors, and the firms that administer or operate retirement plans. They would lose the tools that currently channel benefit disputes into private arbitration, shield them from class litigation, and limit court scrutiny of their benefit decisions. Some of the resulting litigation risk and cost would fall on employers and plan service providers, and defenders of the current system argue some of it may ultimately be borne by plans [S2].

drawbacks.text: Arbitration can be faster and cheaper for an individual worker than a court case; by eliminating mandatory arbitration outright, the bill removes that option even where a worker might privately prefer it, allowing it only after a dispute arises under strict consent conditions [S2].

Employers and plan sponsors argue that expanded litigation rights and class actions raise costs and legal risk for benefit plans, and that some plans respond to litigation risk by reducing offerings or narrowing benefits. The bill does not address how plans would absorb that risk.
Requiring de novo court review of benefit determinations increases litigation over plan interpretation, which could slow down benefit decisions for everyone in a plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees, the benefit is direct and substantial: the ability to enforce their retirement and benefit rights in court, alone or in a group, without fine-print waivers standing in the way. The costs fall mainly on employers and plan administrators through higher litigation exposure, and the objection that some individuals might prefer cheaper arbitration is real but partially answered by the bill, which still permits post-dispute arbitration with genuine consent. The biggest design risk is that plans could respond to new litigation risk in ways that indirectly affect participants.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA) introduced the bill on September 25, 2024 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the first and only step it took [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and no additional actions appear in the record through the end of the Congress [S4].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, including none among House Democrats [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill; it would need to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, plan sponsors, and plan service providers are better off: the arbitration clauses, class-action waivers, and discretionary clauses the bill targeted remain fully enforceable, and their benefit disputes stay out of the courts. Nothing about the current system changed for plan participants either way, because the protections never existed.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the roughly three months it had before the Congress ended

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled the agenda and did not advance the bill at any point before the Congress expired

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one cosponsored the bill, so no partisan divide ever became visible; it simply never moved after referral.

industries.note: These employers currently rely on arbitration clauses, class-action waivers, and discretionary clauses in plan documents to keep benefit disputes out of court and limit their exposure. The bill would strip those protections, leaving them facing ordinary lawsuits over benefits.

industries.industry: Retirement plan administrators and service providers
industries.note: The firms that administer and operate plans would become directly regulated 'covered persons' barred from requiring or agreeing to such waivers, and would face de novo court review of their benefit decisions.
Arbitration firms would lose the stream of ERISA disputes that mandatory clauses steer to them, while plaintiff-side litigation would grow if more participants could sue in court and as classes.
